units.title: Gender
units.intro: Grammar: the past tenses (simple, continuous, perfect) and how they work together in sentences with when, while, before and after.

cards.title: Past tenses (review)
rule: **Past simple** (verb + -ed or irregular form) = a finished action at a past time: *She **won** the race in 2019.*
**Past continuous** (was/were + -ing) = an action in progress at a past moment: *At 8 pm they **were studying**.*
**Past perfect** (had + past participle) = an action that happened **before** another past action: *The film **had started** when we arrived.*

examples.text: I visited my aunt last week.
I was visit my aunt last week.
examples.fix: I visited my aunt last week.

examples.text: When I arrived, the meeting had already begun.
She has finished the work yesterday.

cards.title: Past tenses in adverbial clauses
rule: **Past continuous + past simple:** a longer action interrupted by a short one: *While she **was cooking**, the phone **rang**.*
**Past perfect + past simple:** the earlier action uses the past perfect: *After he **had finished** his homework, he **went** out.*
Use **while** with the longer (continuous) action and **when** usually with the short action.

examples.text: While we were walking home, it started to rain.
While we walked home, it was starting to rain.
examples.fix: While we were walking home, it started to rain.

examples.text: Before the teacher came, we had cleaned the class.

cards.title: Common mistakes
head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: After did, use the base form.
Know is a state verb: no -ing.
Use the past participle after had.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Picture a timeline: **had done** is further back than **did**; **was doing** is the long line, **did** is the short dot that cuts it.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Past simple = finished past action; past continuous = action in progress; past perfect = earlier past action. While + continuous for the long action, when + simple for the short one; the earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.

glossary.meaning: The third form of a verb: gone, written, played.
A clause beginning with when, while, after, before, etc., telling when something happened.

tips.text: Picture a timeline: **had done** is further back than **did**; **was doing** is the long line, **did** is the short dot that cuts it.

units.title: The Internet and You
units.intro: Grammar: active and passive voice in the present, past and future simple, and when to use the passive.

cards.title: Active and passive (1)
rule: In the **active** the subject does the action: *People **use** the Internet.* In the **passive** the subject receives the action: *The Internet **is used** by people.*
**Form:** be (in the right tense) + past participle. Present: is/are + pp; past: was/were + pp; future: will be + pp.
The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive; the doer can be added with **by**.

examples.text: Emails are sent every second.
The message was send yesterday.
The new café will be opened next week.

cards.title: Uses of the passive
rule: Use the passive when the **doer is unknown** (*My phone was stolen.*), when the **receiver is more important** (*The results will be announced on Monday.*), or when the doer is **obvious** (*He was arrested.* — by the police).
Leave out *by + doer* when it adds nothing (*by someone, by people*).

examples.text: Rice is grown in many countries.
Rice is grown by people in many countries.
examples.fix: Rice is grown in many countries.

cards.title: Common mistakes
head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: Be agrees with the new subject.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **BE + 3rd form**: every passive has some form of *be* and the third form of the verb.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Passive = be + past participle; the tense is shown by be (is/are, was/were, will be). Use it when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious; add by + doer only when it matters.

glossary.meaning: A structure where the subject receives the action: be + past participle.
The doer of the action in a passive sentence, introduced by by.

tips.text: **BE + 3rd form**: every passive has some form of *be* and the third form of the verb.

units.title: Self-dependence
units.intro: Grammar: the main parts of speech (nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives) and basic punctuation (full stop, question mark, exclamation mark, comma).

cards.title: Parts of speech (1)
rule: A **noun** names a person, place, thing or idea (*teacher, Keren, book, freedom*). A **pronoun** replaces a noun (*he, she, it, they, him, them*). A **verb** shows an action or state (*run, is, seem*). An **adjective** describes a noun (*a **hard-working** student*).
The same word can be different parts of speech: *a **work** of art* (noun) / *They **work** hard* (verb).

examples.text: She is a confident student.
Him helps his mother.
Freedom is important.

head: Part of speech
Job

I, you, he, it, they, them

cards.title: Punctuation (1)
rule: **Full stop (.)** ends a statement. **Question mark (?)** ends a direct question. **Exclamation mark (!)** shows strong feeling. **Comma (,)** separates items in a list, and follows an introductory word or clause: *However, ...*; *When I arrived, ...*

examples.text: Where do you live?
I bought rice, sugar, oil and salt.
What a beautiful day.

units.title: Love
units.intro: Grammar: linking words that join ideas: and, but, or (conjunctions) and however, moreover, therefore/hence (adverbials).

cards.title: Linking words
rule: **and** adds, **but** contrasts, **or** gives a choice; they join words or clauses inside one sentence: *I love my country **and** I want to serve it.*
**Moreover** (addition), **however** (contrast), **therefore / hence** (result) usually start a new sentence or clause and are followed by a comma: *He was tired. **However**, he kept working.*

examples.text: She was poor but happy.
He studied hard. Therefore, he passed.
He was ill, however he came.
examples.fix: He was ill; however, he came.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Linker
Meaning
Example
rows: It was late but we stayed.
It is cheap. Moreover, it is useful.
It rained. However, we went out.
He trained daily. Therefore, he won.

head: Wrong

He was tired, but he worked.

Therefore needs a cause before it.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Think **A-C-R**: Addition (and, moreover), Contrast (but, however), Result (therefore, hence).

cards.title: Unit summary
body: And/but/or join ideas inside one sentence. Moreover (addition), however (contrast) and therefore/hence (result) link sentences and take a comma after them.

glossary.meaning: A word that joins words or clauses: and, but, or.
A word like however or therefore that links sentences.

tips.text: Think **A-C-R**: Addition (and, moreover), Contrast (but, however), Result (therefore, hence).

units.title: Politeness
units.intro: Grammar: reported (indirect) speech for statements, questions, requests and commands, and punctuation marks (colon, semi-colon, brackets, hyphen, apostrophe, quotation marks).

cards.title: Reported speech
rule: When the reporting verb is past (*said, asked, told*), the tense usually moves **one step back**: am/is → was; present simple → past simple; past simple → past perfect; will → would; can → could.
Pronouns and time words change: *now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there*.
**Questions:** *asked + if/whether* (yes/no) or *asked + wh-word*, with **statement word order** and no question mark. **Requests/commands:** *asked/told + object + (not) to + verb*.

examples.text: She said that she was tired.
He asked me where did I live.
examples.fix: He asked me where I lived.

examples.text: The teacher told us to sit down.
She told me don’t go.
examples.fix: She told me not to go.

cards.pattern: said (that) + backshift  ·  asked if/wh- + statement order  ·  told + obj + to-inf

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Direct
Reported
rows: She asked if I liked tea.
She asked me to help her.
He told us not to shout.

cards.title: Punctuation (2)
rule: **Quotation marks** enclose the exact words in direct speech: *“I’m sorry,” she said.* **Apostrophe** shows possession (*Meron’s bag*) or a missing letter (*don’t*). **Colon (:)** introduces a list or explanation. **Semi-colon (;)** joins two closely related sentences. **Hyphen (-)** joins compound words (*well-known*). **Brackets ( )** add extra information.

examples.text: “Please wait,” the clerk said.
The boys bags are here.

cards.title: Common mistakes
head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: He asked me what was my name?
He asked me what my name was.
She told me that... / She said that...
Tell + person; say without a person.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **One step back** in time, **statement order** for questions, **to-verb** for orders.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: In reported speech the tense moves back after a past reporting verb, pronouns and time words change, questions use if/whether or a wh-word with statement order, and requests or commands use asked/told + object + (not) to + verb.

glossary.meaning: Telling what someone said without using their exact words.
Moving a verb one tense back in reported speech.

tips.text: **One step back** in time, **statement order** for questions, **to-verb** for orders.

units.title: Making Friends
units.intro: Grammar: subject–verb agreement (including neither/nor, either/or, together with) and the other parts of speech: adverbs, conjunctions, prepositions and interjections.

cards.title: Subject–verb agreement
rule: A singular subject takes a singular verb (*My friend **lives** here*); a plural subject takes a plural verb (*My friends **live** here*).
With **either ... or** and **neither ... nor**, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: *Neither the teacher nor the **students are** here.* / *Either the students or the **teacher is** here.*
**Together with, as well as, along with** do not change the subject: *The captain, together with his players, **is** coming.* **Each, every, everyone, nobody** take a singular verb.

Neither Ali nor his brothers is at home.

cards.title: Parts of speech (2)
rule: An **adverb** describes a verb, adjective or another adverb (*She speaks **frankly***; *very* tall). Many adverbs = adjective + **-ly** (*happy → happily, easy → easily, late → lately* (= recently)). A **conjunction** joins (*and, because, although*). A **preposition** shows place, time or relation (*in, on, at, apart from*). An **interjection** shows feeling (*Oh! Wow! Ouch!*).

She sings beautiful.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Singular subjects take singular verbs and plural subjects plural verbs. With either/or and neither/nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; phrases like together with do not change the subject. Adverbs describe verbs (often -ly); prepositions, conjunctions and interjections complete the parts of speech.

units.title: Energy
units.intro: Grammar: noun phrases with articles (a/an/the/zero), singular and plural nouns, and tag questions with be, do, have and will.

cards.title: Articles and noun phrases
rule: Use **a** before a consonant sound and **an** before a vowel sound with singular countable nouns mentioned for the first time: *a solar panel, an hour, a university*.
Use **the** when the noun is known or unique: *the sun, the energy we used, the Red Sea*.
Use **no article** (zero) with plural or uncountable nouns in general: *Energy is expensive. Trees give shade.*

examples.text: The sun gives us energy.
She bought an uniform.

cards.title: Tag questions
rule: A **tag question** checks information. A **positive** statement takes a **negative** tag; a negative statement takes a positive tag. Use the same auxiliary (be, do, have, will, can): *You are tired, **aren’t you**? She doesn’t eat meat, **does she**?*
Special: *I am ..., **aren’t I**? Let’s go, **shall we**?* After *nobody, nothing* use a positive tag: *Nobody came, **did they**?*

examples.text: It will rain, won’t it?
He likes tea, isn’t he?

cards.title: Unit summary
body: A/an for one countable thing mentioned first (by sound), the for known or unique things, zero article for general plurals and uncountables. Tag questions reverse the statement’s polarity and repeat its auxiliary.

cards.title: Passive in continuous and perfect tenses
rule: **Present continuous passive:** am/is/are + **being** + past participle: *The road **is being repaired**.*

**Present perfect passive:** has/have + **been** + pp: *The results **have been published**.* **Past perfect passive:** had + **been** + pp: *The tickets **had been sold** before we came.*

units.title: Population and Our Future
units.intro: Grammar: talking about the future and conditional sentences type 1 (real/possible) and type 2 (unreal/imaginary).

cards.title: Conditionals type 1 and 2
rule: **Type 1 (real possibility):** *If + present simple, will + base verb.* *If the population **grows** fast, we **will need** more schools.*

**Type 2 (unreal or unlikely now/future):** *If + past simple, would + base verb.* *If I **had** more land, I **would grow** more food.* With be, use **were** for all persons in formal English: *If I **were** you, ...*
The if-clause can come second; then no comma: *We will need more schools if the population grows.*

units.intro: Grammar: the third conditional for imagining a different past.

cards.title: Conditional type 3
rule: **Form:** *If + past perfect, would have + past participle.* *If she **had studied**, she **would have passed**.*

**Meaning:** an imaginary past: the condition did **not** happen, so the result did not happen either. It is often used for regrets: *If I **had known** about my fear of heights, I **wouldn’t have climbed** the tower.*
Could have / might have can replace would have: *If we had left earlier, we **might have caught** the bus.*

why: If-clause of type 3: had + past participle.
questions.tip: Say the sentence aloud with your answer; it must be grammatical and make sense.
